screens.title: Introduction to Cisco SD-Access
screens.narratorSegment: Software-Defined Access or SD-Access rethinks the campus network by treating connectivity, policy, and device identity as programmable services. Instead of treating switches and VLANs as static building blocks, SD-Access separates the physical transport that provides IP reachability from a virtual overlay that delivers segmentation, host mobility, and consistent policy. This matters because modern networks need to support mobile users, IoT devices, and rapid service rollouts without long manual change windows. In practice that means you can create logical segments that move with users, enforce identity-based access consistently, and automate provisioning from a central controller. A concrete example is giving a contractor temporary access: with SD-Access you assign a security group tag at authentication, and the fabric enforces the right rules across wired and wireless without touching switch configurations individually. A common misconception is to troubleshoot overlay problems with underlay commands; the underlay provides reachability while the overlay delivers host identity and policy. As you begin this chapter, notice how the architecture splits roles—management, control, data, and policy—so each can be automated and validated independently. Think about one service you manage today and how identity-based, automated policy could reduce errors and speed deployment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why enterprises adopt SD-Access, identify the fabric's key components, and describe how the underlay and overlay separate responsibilities. You will interpret how VXLAN and LISP work together to provide host mobility, and you will explain how Cisco TrustSec uses Security Group Tags for consistent policy enforcement. These skills matter because they let you design and operate fabric networks without conflating physical transport with logical policy. A concrete example: after this chapter, you will be able to justify moving from VLAN-based segmentation to an overlay-based approach when users and devices move frequently across access points. A common trap to avoid is treating diagnostic commands for the underlay as if they reveal overlay state; the two planes require different tooling and mapping techniques. Finally, you will practice identifying components in a sample topology so you can map real equipment roles to SD-Access functions in your environment. Consider which objective would reduce your operational risk most, and focus your study on how that component integrates with DNA Center and ISE.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives page focuses on operational skills and common pitfalls. You will learn to plan IP addressing for underlay loopbacks and overlay virtual networks, and to validate that LISP mappings are updating when hosts move. You will also practice reasoning about policy decisions made in ISE and enforced at the Fabric Edge, including how Security Group Tags translate into SGACLs. A practical example is planning loopback addressing so every fabric device can reach each other without address overlap; this prevents routing confusion between underlay and overlay. A common mistake is assuming DNA Center will automatically correct every design problem. DNA Center automates many tasks, but it still depends on accurate planning and verified templates. Finally, the objectives ask you to be able to recognize when to test configuration changes in a lab first, because automation can propagate mistakes rapidly. Keep these operational checks in mind as you study each component; they are the difference between a theoretical design and a resilient production deployment.

screens.title: Why SD-Access: motivations and benefits
screens.narratorSegment: SD-Access addresses the operational pain of static, manually configured campus networks by introducing automation, logical segmentation, and identity-based policy. The claim is simple: when you separate management, control, data, and policy planes and centralize common actions, you reduce configuration inconsistency and speed provisioning. For example, instead of configuring VLANs and ACLs on many switches for a new user group, DNA Center lets you define a segment and push consistent settings across the fabric. An immediate benefit is host mobility: users retain their segment and policy when they move between access points or switches. A practical example is onboarding a fleet of IoT sensors. With SD-Access you can assign them to a security group once in ISE and have that group enforced everywhere, rather than manually adjusting many switch ports. A common misconception is that SD-Access removes the need to plan addressing or understand routing. It does not; the underlay still requires correct IP design. The takeaway is that SD-Access lowers manual effort and enforces consistency, but it must be paired with solid planning and validation. Ask yourself which repetitive tasks in your network would most benefit from automation and identity-based enforcement.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Why SD-Access
Definition
SD-Access automates provisioning, delivers logical segmentation, and enforces identity-based policy across wired and wireless access.
Automation: design once, provision many devices consistently.
Segmentation: logical groups follow users, enabling micro-segmentation.
Identity: policies tied to Security Group Tags, not IP addresses.
Key takeaway
SD-Access reduces manual configuration and enforces consistent security across the campus.
Concrete example
Onboarding contractors or IoT: assign an SGT in ISE once, and the fabric enforces access everywhere without per-switch changes.
Problem: manual VLAN changes
SD-Access: define segment centrally
Result: consistent enforcement
Common mistake: treating SD-Access as a silver bullet. It streamlines operations but requires planning for addressing, policy design, and template validation.

screens.title: Underlay vs Overlay
screens.narratorSegment: Underlay and overlay are the two foundational planes in SD-Access. The underlay is the IP-based transport fabric that provides reachability between devices. It uses traditional routing protocols and loopback addressing to ensure every fabric device can exchange packets. The overlay is the virtualized layer that provides logical networks, host mobility, and policy enforcement by encapsulating endpoint traffic. A concrete example: VXLAN encapsulates Ethernet frames so a virtual network can span switches without VLAN limits, while the underlay routes the VXLAN packets between devices. A common misconception is to assume that underlay routing errors always mean overlay failure. In reality, overlay issues can exist even when the underlay is healthy, and vice versa. For troubleshooting, verify underlay reachability first, then inspect overlay control mappings. Practical significance: planning underlay loopbacks and routing ensures VXLAN tunnels can be established reliably. Try a mental check: if two fabric nodes cannot exchange VXLAN packets, ask whether their loopbacks are reachable in the underlay before changing overlay mappings. This simple discipline prevents misdirected troubleshooting and speeds resolution. Underlay vs Overlay means underlay offers ip transport; overlay provides virtual networks and host mobility via encapsulation and mappings.. In practical terms, clear separation of transport and virtual services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Underlay vs Overlay
Underlay (Transport)
  • Provides IP reachability between fabric devices.
  • Uses loopback addressing and routing protocols for transport.
  • Must be designed carefully for stability and reachability.
Example: ensure loopbacks are reachable so VXLAN packets traverse the fabric.
Overlay (Virtualization)
  • Provides logical segmentation, host mobility, and policy.
  • Uses VXLAN for encapsulation and LISP for location mappings.
  • Independent from physical topology; virtual networks span devices.
Example: a VN carried by VXLAN lets a host keep its IP when it moves across edges.
Troubleshoot: confirm underlay reachability before investigating overlay control mappings.
Misconception: overlay problems are not always visible via underlay commands.
Takeaway: separate checks for underlay and overlay speed diagnosis.

screens.title: Key SD-Access Components
screens.narratorSegment: SD-Access is a collection of components that collaborate to deliver automation, control, and policy. DNA Center acts as the orchestration and automation engine: it designs, provisions, and assures the fabric. Cisco ISE is the policy decision point, authenticating users and devices and assigning Security Group Tags. Fabric Edge Nodes are the access-layer switches where endpoints attach; they encapsulate and decapsulate VXLAN and enforce SGACLs. Fabric Border Nodes connect the fabric to external networks like the data center or internet and translate between fabric and non-fabric domains. Fabric Control Plane Nodes maintain endpoint location information using LISP mappings, supporting host mobility. Wireless LAN Controllers are integrated so wireless clients receive the same segmentation and policy as wired endpoints. A concrete scenario: when a client authenticates, ISE assigns an SGT, the Edge enforces associated access control, and the Control Plane ensures traffic is routed to the client's current location. A common misconception is that DNA Center performs all policy decisions. DNA Center provisions and automates; ISE remains the policy authority, and edge nodes enforce policy at the data plane. Remember each component's responsibility to design and operate a resilient fabric.

keyIdea.title: Component roles
keyIdea.text: DNA Center automates, ISE decides policy, Edge enforces, Border connects out, Control Plane tracks locations, WLC extends wireless into the fabric.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › SD-Access Components
Component cards
DNA Center: provisioning, design templates, and assurance.
ISE: authentication and SGT assignment for policy.
Fabric Edge: access switches that encapsulate/decapsulate and enforce SGACLs.
Fabric Border: connects fabric to external networks and translates domains.
Control Plane Node: maintains EID-to-RLOC mappings via LISP.
WLC: integrates wireless clients into the fabric with consistent policy.
Flow example
Client authenticates → ISE assigns SGT → DNA Center ensures templates are in place → Edge enforces SGACLs → Control Plane updates mappings for mobility.
Misconception check: DNA Center orchestrates but ISE remains the policy decision point; enforcement happens at the Edge.

screens.title: VXLAN in SD-Access
screens.narratorSegment: VXLAN is the data plane encapsulation used by SD-Access overlays. Its role is to carry endpoint Ethernet frames inside UDP packets so that virtual networks can span multiple physical switches without the constraints of traditional VLANs. Practically, VXLAN lets you have many distinct virtual networks across the campus, each isolated even if endpoints are on different physical devices. For example, a finance VN and a guest VN can coexist and be kept separate while traversing the same underlay routers. A common misconception is that VXLAN changes how you do IP addressing for endpoints; it doesn't alter endpoint addressing but wraps frames for transport. VXLAN depends on a reliable underlay: if the underlay cannot forward VXLAN-encapsulated packets between fabric nodes, the overlay fails. The takeaway is that VXLAN provides flexible Layer 2 emulation over Layer 3 and is a cornerstone for mobility and large-scale segmentation in SD-Access. When designing overlays, consider how VN boundaries map to policy and how encapsulation affects MTU sizing and underlay routing. VXLAN in SD-Access means vxlan encapsulates ethernet frames so virtual networks can span the fabric independently of physical topology.. In practical terms, encapsulation that enables virtual networks across the fabric. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › VXLAN
How VXLAN works
VXLAN takes a normal Ethernet frame and encapsulates it in a UDP/IP packet. This allows a virtual network to be extended across an IP underlay so endpoints can keep their Layer 2 attributes independent of the physical switch layout.
Encapsulation: Ethernet → VXLAN over UDP
Uses VN identifiers to separate traffic
Enables host mobility across fabric edges
Design note: confirm underlay MTU and reachability to carry VXLAN frames reliably.
Example
A user moves from one access switch to another. VXLAN ensures their virtual network membership remains intact while the underlay forwards the encapsulated packets between fabric nodes.
Misconception: VXLAN replaces routing. It extends Layer 2 but still relies on the underlay IP routing for transport.

screens.title: LISP and the Control Plane
screens.narratorSegment: LISP is the control plane technology in SD-Access that separates endpoint identifiers from their routing locations. The key idea is that a host's identity or endpoint ID is decoupled from the physical locator of the device serving it. LISP maintains a mapping database so that when an endpoint moves, its new location is recorded and traffic can still reach it without changing the underlay. For a concrete example, imagine a laptop moving from one access switch to another. The Control Plane Node updates the EID-to-RLOC mapping so ongoing sessions continue without manual reconfiguration. A common misconception is that moving a host requires new routing entries everywhere; LISP centralizes mapping updates so only the mapping service needs to notify reachability changes. Operationally, you will verify mapping updates during mobility tests and ensure the control-plane nodes are reachable and synchronized. The takeaway is that LISP provides scalable host mobility and reduces the need to modify underlay routing as hosts move across the fabric. LISP and the Control Plane means lisp provides a scalable mapping service that tracks endpoint locations so hosts move without changing routing tables across the underlay.. In practical terms, mapping endpoint identifiers to routing locators for mobility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › LISP (Control Plane)
Concept
LISP maps endpoint identifiers (EIDs) to routing locators (RLOCs). This mapping allows the fabric to route traffic to the current location of a host without changing underlay routes.
Example: laptop moves, LISP updates EID→RLOC so sessions continue seamlessly.
Operational notes
  • Ensure control plane nodes are reachable in the underlay.
  • Monitor mapping updates during mobility tests.
  • Keep mapping databases consistent across control nodes.
Misconception: LISP replaces policy. It maps locations; policy enforcement is handled via SGTs and SGACLs at the Edge.

screens.title: Cisco TrustSec and Security Group Tags (SGTs)
screens.narratorSegment: Cisco TrustSec provides the policy plane for SD-Access by using Security Group Tags to classify users and devices. Instead of writing access controls tied to IP addresses, you assign an SGT when a device authenticates, and policies reference that tag to permit or deny traffic. For a concrete example, an SGT for contractors can restrict them to internet access and deny access to internal finance systems, regardless of the contractor's current IP or physical switch. ISE is the policy decision point that authenticates and assigns SGTs; the Fabric Edge enforces SGACLs derived from those tags. A misconception to avoid is thinking SGTs are only useful for security auditing. They are active enforcement primitives across the fabric that enable consistent micro-segmentation. Operationally, verify that ISE assignments propagate to edge devices and that SGACLs behave as expected in test scenarios. The takeaway is that SGT-based policy simplifies management by decoupling policy from IP addressing and topology, making segmentation scalable and less error-prone. Cisco TrustSec and Security Group Tags (SGTs) means sgts let you define policy by identity group, enabling consistent enforcement as devices move across the fabric.. In practical terms, identity-based policy and consistent enforcement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › TrustSec & SGTs
Policy concept
An SGT is a tag assigned by ISE that classifies a user or device. Policies reference SGTs, not IPs, so enforcement is consistent across the fabric.
Use case: contractors get limited access regardless of location.
Use case: IoT devices placed in a single policy group for monitoring and isolation.
Operational checks
  • Confirm ISE assigns expected SGTs after authentication.
  • Confirm Edge devices enforce SGACLs associated with tags.
  • Test policy before broad deployment to avoid accidental blocking.
Misconception: SGTs remove the need for testing. Always validate SGACLs as automation can propagate errors quickly.

screens.title: Authentication to Enforcement Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the flow from authentication to enforcement clarifies where decisions are made and where enforcement occurs. The process begins when a device attaches to a Fabric Edge and authenticates. Cisco ISE performs authentication and assigns an SGT based on policy. That SGT is communicated to the Edge, which applies the corresponding SGACLs in the data plane. DNA Center automates provisioning and ensures templates and policies are distributed correctly, but it is not the policy decision point. The Control Plane keeps mappings to ensure traffic reaches the device's current RLOC. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying SD-Access brings automation benefits but also requires discipline to avoid costly mistakes. Common errors include insufficient IP planning for underlay loopbacks and overlay virtual networks, trying to troubleshoot overlays with underlay commands, and applying untested policy templates at scale. Best practices begin with careful addressing design for loopbacks and management interfaces so every fabric device is reachable. Next, run thorough lab tests for policy changes and automation templates; automation propagates errors quickly, so test before production. Verify that ISE assignments map to expected SGACLs on Edge devices and that Control Plane nodes are reachable and synchronizing mappings. Back up DNA Center and ISE configurations and document your template versions. A concrete example: a misapplied SGACL that blocks an essential service can be propagated by automation to every Edge, causing a widespread outage. A recovery guard is staged testing and rollback-ready templates. The practical takeaway is to pair SD-Access automation with rigorous planning and validation. Ask: do my templates have safe defaults and rollback steps? If not, add that control before automating broadly. fullNarratorScript:
Software-Defined Access or SD-Access rethinks the campus network by treating connectivity, policy, and device identity as programmable services. Instead of treating switches and VLANs as static building blocks, SD-Access separates the physical transport that provides IP reachability from a virtual overlay that delivers segmentation, host mobility, and consistent policy. This matters because modern networks need to support mobile users, IoT devices, and rapid service rollouts without long manual change windows. In practice that means you can create logical segments that move with users, enforce identity-based access consistently, and automate provisioning from a central controller. A concrete example is giving a contractor temporary access: with SD-Access you assign a security group tag at authentication, and the fabric enforces the right rules across wired and wireless without touching switch configurations individually. A common misconception is to troubleshoot overlay problems with underlay commands; the underlay provides reachability while the overlay delivers host identity and policy. As you begin this chapter, notice how the architecture splits roles—management, control, data, and policy—so each can be automated and validated independently. Think about one service you manage today and how identity-based, automated policy could reduce errors and speed deployment.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why enterprises adopt SD-Access, identify the fabric's key components, and describe how the underlay and overlay separate responsibilities. You will interpret how VXLAN and LISP work together to provide host mobility, and you will explain how Cisco TrustSec uses Security Group Tags for consistent policy enforcement. These skills matter because they let you design and operate fabric networks without conflating physical transport with logical policy. A concrete example: after this chapter, you will be able to justify moving from VLAN-based segmentation to an overlay-based approach when users and devices move frequently across access points. A common trap to avoid is treating diagnostic commands for the underlay as if they reveal overlay state; the two planes require different tooling and mapping techniques. Finally, you will practice identifying components in a sample topology so you can map real equipment roles to SD-Access functions in your environment. Consider which objective would reduce your operational risk most, and focus your study on how that component integrates with DNA Center and ISE.

This second objectives page focuses on operational skills and common pitfalls. You will learn to plan IP addressing for underlay loopbacks and overlay virtual networks, and to validate that LISP mappings are updating when hosts move. You will also practice reasoning about policy decisions made in ISE and enforced at the Fabric Edge, including how Security Group Tags translate into SGACLs. A practical example is planning loopback addressing so every fabric device can reach each other without address overlap; this prevents routing confusion between underlay and overlay. A common mistake is assuming DNA Center will automatically correct every design problem. DNA Center automates many tasks, but it still depends on accurate planning and verified templates. Finally, the objectives ask you to be able to recognize when to test configuration changes in a lab first, because automation can propagate mistakes rapidly. Keep these operational checks in mind as you study each component; they are the difference between a theoretical design and a resilient production deployment.

SD-Access addresses the operational pain of static, manually configured campus networks by introducing automation, logical segmentation, and identity-based policy. The claim is simple: when you separate management, control, data, and policy planes and centralize common actions, you reduce configuration inconsistency and speed provisioning. For example, instead of configuring VLANs and ACLs on many switches for a new user group, DNA Center lets you define a segment and push consistent settings across the fabric. An immediate benefit is host mobility: users retain their segment and policy when they move between access points or switches. A practical example is onboarding a fleet of IoT sensors. With SD-Access you can assign them to a security group once in ISE and have that group enforced everywhere, rather than manually adjusting many switch ports. A common misconception is that SD-Access removes the need to plan addressing or understand routing. It does not; the underlay still requires correct IP design. The takeaway is that SD-Access lowers manual effort and enforces consistency, but it must be paired with solid planning and validation. Ask yourself which repetitive tasks in your network would most benefit from automation and identity-based enforcement.

Underlay and overlay are the two foundational planes in SD-Access. The underlay is the IP-based transport fabric that provides reachability between devices. It uses traditional routing protocols and loopback addressing to ensure every fabric device can exchange packets. The overlay is the virtualized layer that provides logical networks, host mobility, and policy enforcement by encapsulating endpoint traffic. A concrete example: VXLAN encapsulates Ethernet frames so a virtual network can span switches without VLAN limits, while the underlay routes the VXLAN packets between devices. A common misconception is to assume that underlay routing errors always mean overlay failure. In reality, overlay issues can exist even when the underlay is healthy, and vice versa. For troubleshooting, verify underlay reachability first, then inspect overlay control mappings. Practical significance: planning underlay loopbacks and routing ensures VXLAN tunnels can be established reliably. Try a mental check: if two fabric nodes cannot exchange VXLAN packets, ask whether their loopbacks are reachable in the underlay before changing overlay mappings. This simple discipline prevents misdirected troubleshooting and speeds resolution. Underlay vs Overlay means underlay offers ip transport; overlay provides virtual networks and host mobility via encapsulation and mappings.. In practical terms, clear separation of transport and virtual services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SD-Access is a collection of components that collaborate to deliver automation, control, and policy. DNA Center acts as the orchestration and automation engine: it designs, provisions, and assures the fabric. Cisco ISE is the policy decision point, authenticating users and devices and assigning Security Group Tags. Fabric Edge Nodes are the access-layer switches where endpoints attach; they encapsulate and decapsulate VXLAN and enforce SGACLs. Fabric Border Nodes connect the fabric to external networks like the data center or internet and translate between fabric and non-fabric domains. Fabric Control Plane Nodes maintain endpoint location information using LISP mappings, supporting host mobility. Wireless LAN Controllers are integrated so wireless clients receive the same segmentation and policy as wired endpoints. A concrete scenario: when a client authenticates, ISE assigns an SGT, the Edge enforces associated access control, and the Control Plane ensures traffic is routed to the client's current location. VXLAN is the data plane encapsulation used by SD-Access overlays. Its role is to carry endpoint Ethernet frames inside UDP packets so that virtual networks can span multiple physical switches without the constraints of traditional VLANs. Practically, VXLAN lets you have many distinct virtual networks across the campus, each isolated even if endpoints are on different physical devices.
